You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failing test calls StrBuilder.deleteFirst("three") on a StrBuilder initialized with "onetwothree". The test then asserts that "three" is no longer found in the StrBuilder by checking indexOf("three") returns -1.

Looking at the code:
- StrBuilder.deleteFirst(String) finds the index of the first occurrence of the string and calls deleteImpl to remove that substring. It then returns the StrBuilder.
- StrBuilder.indexOf(String, int) looks for the first occurrence of the given substring starting at the given index. It returns the index or -1 if not found.
- StrBuilder.deleteImpl(int startIndex, int endIndex, int len) removes chars between startIndex and endIndex and reduces the size by len.
- There is a related method StrBuilder.deleteAll(String) which deletes all occurrences of a string by repeatedly finding the index and calling deleteImpl, until no more occurrences are found.

The current bug report mentions that deleteAll and replaceAll can throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Inspecting the deleteAll method code, it repeatedly deletes substrings, and each time calls indexOf(str, index) to find next occurrence starting from the same index. This can cause skipping elements deletion or infinite loop, which may lead to out of bounds when the internal size decreases but indexOf uses buffer.length for boundary check.

Comparing this to deleteFirst, it only deletes the first occurrence once, so the failure likely comes from the mismatch of buffer.length and size in indexOf and deleteImpl leading to wrong bounds. The indexOf method calculates a variable "len" as thisBuf.length - strLen instead of using size - strLen, meaning it searches beyond the current valid size of buffer, especially after deletions. This causes incorrect indexing if buffer is bigger than size after deletions. This can cause indexOf to return an invalid index, which when passed to deleteImpl can cause ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

The test `testIndexOfLang294` expects indexOf after deleting "three" to return -1, indicating "three" is no longer present, but due to the above flaw, it might still find an occurrence because indexOf checks beyond current size. Thus the assertion fails.

In summary:
- indexOf uses buffer.length instead of size when checking substring boundaries.
- After deletion, size is reduced but buffer length remains same, so indexOf may search beyond valid characters.
- This causes indexOf to incorrectly find substrings that are not valid or out of current size bounds.
- deleteFirst depends on indexOf, so it cannot reliably confirm that substring was deleted.
- This relates to the current bug report about deleteAll and replaceAll throwing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException since similar use of indexOf happens there.
- Fix is to use size instead of buffer.length in indexOf method for boundary checks.

The recent bug reports are not relevant to this issue as they concern other classes and methods.

Overall, the root cause is that indexOf(String,int) uses buffer.length instead of size field when limiting the search range, causing invalid indexing after deletions which modify size but not buffer.length.

Best places to fix are indexOf and potentially the deleteAll and deleteFirst methods to ensure correct bounds usage. Also deleteImpl should be safe but the bug arises before calls to it.

This explains why the test fails and matches the symptoms in the bug report.
org.apache.commons.lang.text.StrBuilder.indexOf(java.lang.String,int)
org.apache.commons.lang.text.StrBuilder.deleteAll(java.lang.String)
org.apache.commons.lang.text.StrBuilder.deleteFirst(java.lang.String)

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
